content: This regulation forms the legal bedrock for all crane safety protocols in the country. Furthermore, the Construction Regulations, also under the OHSA, impose additional duties when cranes are used on a construction site. These regulations require the principal contractor to ensure that any subcontractor, such as a crane hire company, is compliant with the OHSA. They mandate the development of a site-specific health and safety plan, which must incorporate all lifting operations. This creates a chain of responsibility, meaning Veralift is not only accountable to the Department of Employment and Labour but also contractually accountable to its clients (the principal contractors) for its safety performance. Environmental regulations, such as the National Environmental Management Act (NEMA), also play a role, particularly concerning potential environmental impacts like soil contamination from hydraulic fluid spills or noise pollution, requiring operators to have appropriate mitigation procedures in place. Labour laws, including the Basic Conditions of Employment Act, govern working hours, overtime, and rest periods for crane operators and rigging crews, which must be factored into project planning to ensure legal compliance and prevent fatigue-related accidents. Certifications are the tangible proof of compliance and competence within this regulatory system. Veralift must maintain a meticulous register of all equipment, tracking inspection and certification expiry dates to ensure its entire fleet remains compliant at all times. This register is one of the first documents requested during a safety audit by either a client or a Department of Labour inspector. Personnel certifications are equally critical. Crane operators must undergo formal training and assessment at an accredited training institution. Upon successful completion, they receive a certificate of competence that specifies the type and capacity of crane they are qualified to operate. This is not a one-size-fits-all certification; an operator certified for a 50-tonne all-terrain crane is not automatically qualified to operate a 200-tonne crawler crane. Veralift's human resources and operations departments must manage a database of operator qualifications to ensure the correct operator is assigned to each machine and task. Similarly, riggers, the individuals responsible for attaching the load to the crane, must also be trained and certified.
